Editor's Note: This is the final volume of the series, recording a lecture by Mo Li of the Gongyang Family in Aerux Town. He elaborates on the appreciation and critique of music. Music is not just a cold art, but an expression of inner emotions. Through appreciation and critique, we can gain a deeper understanding of the stories and emotions behind musical works, and feel the composers' intentions and pursuits. 
 
 
 
Here is the full text of Master Mo Li's lecture. 
 
 
 
Greetings to everyone in Aerux Town. 
 
 
 
Today, I'd like to talk about the appreciation and critique of music. As an art form, music has a unique charm and infectious power. Learning to appreciate and critique music can help us better grasp its beauty and deeper meanings. 
 
 
 
Appreciation involves enjoying and analyzing music. When we appreciate music, we usually start with melody, rhythm, harmony, timbre, and other aspects. Some people say that the Gongyang Family seems too formal, making it intimidating to communicate with them. However, most members of the Gongyang Family are eager for others to appreciate their music. If you ever meet a member of the Gongyang Family with a questioning gaze, feel free to share your thoughts. 
 
 
 
Melody is the soul of music, and a beautiful melody can captivate anyone. Rhythm is the backbone of music, giving it dynamism and vitality. Mastering the rhythm allows every note to touch the heart, making the performance flow smoothly. 
 
 
 
Harmony enriches the layering and depth of music. In addition to the main melody, harmony is also a crucial element, with specialized courses at Jixia Academy. 
 
 
 
Timbre is the color of music, with different instruments and sounds adding rich colors. Among the instruments commonly used by the Gongyang Family, you can see various instruments such as the guqin, flute, and pipa. Each instrument has a unique timbre, weaving together to form a beautiful musical landscape. 
 
 
 
The Gongyang Family often performs in the Garden of Delight, where you can experience the melody, rhythm, harmony, and timbre of their music. 
 
 
 
Moreover, we can also approach music from its content. In the philosophy of Jixia Academy, the music of the Gongyang Family emphasizes not only technical skill but also emotional expression. Through their music, they convey their insights into life, their reverence for nature, and their reflections on human nature. 
 
 
 
When we appreciate music, we can use appreciation to understand the intentions and techniques of composers and performers, feeling the emotions and atmosphere conveyed by the music. Furthermore, we can also combine our own feelings and experiences to interpret and reflect on the music. 
 
 
 
In summary, the appreciation and critique of music vary with each listener. If a piece of music resonates with you, share your insights and feelings with the Gongyang Family in the Garden of Delight. I believe that in the vast world of Jixia, you will surely find someone who shares your musical sensibility. 
 
 
 
Editor's Note: The five lectures by Master Mo Li have been compiled, and readers should now have their own understanding of the Gongyang Family. This group stands out among the Society for their unique existence; they neither shine in practical fields like the Artisan or Cannons, nor do they focus on daily life like the Hunters or Anglers. Instead, they are elegant and introspective, playing the guqin to praise hidden chapters buried by time and to soothe the spiritual fatigue of workers. They are a vibrant tapestry in the sprawling architectural complexes, accentuating the splendor of the city.

This supplement to the Saepes Compendium, authored by the Hunter, Mu Ping, documents the origins and distributions of the Saepes. 
The Saepes are trees. That is no lie. They are a peculiar kind of creature that originated from plants. Although they have many animal-like traits, it must be noted they are still considered plants. The Saepes are widespread throughout Jixia and have evolved into many subspecies. 
In Jixia, the competition among the numerous plant species is fierce. Simply put, plants need sunlight and water to thrive. Those that grow taller garner more resources. Otherwise, they must either subsist under the shade of others or perish. Moreover, the Aercocoons atop the Tower of Enlightenment emit Aerflow that, upon descending, transforms into Jixia's unique Aersilk. This phenomenon, still under study, suggests that Aersilk provides nutrients far superior to sunlight and water, offering a vitality that makes it a coveted resource. 
In this botanical battleground, the Saepes are the winners. Research indicates that their ancestors triumphed in an ancient competition for height, absorbing more Aersilk than other plants. The life essence in the Aersilk evolved them into sentient plant beings. We refer to these ancestors as "the Primary Saepes." 
Analysis shows that all Saepes in Jixia descend from this ancestor that evolved the ability to move rather than stay rooted. Evidence of this Primary Saepes' travels is abundant in Springbrook Plains, where we've found numerous fossilized footprints (refer to the sketch below). 
As the Primary Saepes roamed, it scattered seeds along its path. While some offspring grew into traditional Saepes trees, others inherited the mobility and rudimentary intelligence of their ancestor, spreading across Jixia over generations. It's unclear how many generations have passed, but Saepes have existed in Jixia far longer than humans and other settlers. 
Beyond Springbrook Plains, Saepes are found throughout Jixia, from Mount Guye in the northwest to Iridescent Basin in the northeast, and from Aerfall Highlands to Dreamweave Plains, including Jixia Mountain. However, they are notably scarce in certain southern parts of Jixia Mountain, suggesting a natural aversion that begs further investigation. 
Note: This phenomenon was confirmed firsthand last month when Senior Wuxin and I were chased by Saepes after they spotted us collecting seeds outside the Academy. They chased us for several miles but abruptly stopped once we reached the backhill. It's no surprise, given how obsolete this area is.

In an unfamiliar outdoor environment, lacking direction-indicating tools like a south-pointing needle makes it very easy to lose your way. But do not worry; we have many methods to help you regain your bearings. Note, however, that while searching for direction, you should use items like stones and branches to leave road signs and prevent walking in circles. 
 
Method One: Observe celestial bodies. During the day, you can determine direction by observing the position of the sun, which rises in the east and sets in the west, with minor shifts depending on the seasonal changes. At night, you can observe the position of the moon or the North Star to tell direction. Observing the changes in the sun and moon also allows you to track time changes so you can return to your shelter before dark. Familiarity with astrological patterns is also a very important method for determining direction. 
 
However, this method has major limitations. In some special environments, we cannot observe celestial bodies to judge direction—for instance, on rainy days or in heavily sheltered spaces like deep mountain forests. 
 
Method Two: Judge direction based on your surrounding environment. For example, if you find Aervein crystal ore nearby, you can place a small amount of Aersilk on the crystal ore, and the Aersilk will automatically gather toward the direction of the-Tower-to-Heaven. Secondly, Jixia's overall terrain is higher in the west and lower in the east; you can stand on high ground to observe the nearby terrain. If there are distinct undulating mountains and staggered zones, it is easy to distinguish east and west. If you are in a relatively low river valley plain area, you can observe the river's flow. Influenced by the terrain, most of Jixia's water flows from west to east, which can also be used to roughly determine direction. 
 
Method Three: Determine direction through the characteristics of flora and fauna. For instance, you can judge direction by observing the growth orientation of plants; flowers and fruits of plants like Zhaoxun fruit usually grow southward. You can also observe fruit color, with the side facing south having a deeper fruit color. If there happens to be Deng Hua grass nearby, you can try scattering it, and the scattered light within will automatically float toward the river. Follow it to find the river, walk along the river to the plain river valley area, and you will often find densely populated villages. 
 
Finally, if you are in a desperate situation, try every possible means to send signals to the outside world, such as producing light, thick smoke, or special odors. With luck, you might encounter wilderness adventure naturalists and hunters. No matter what, do not give up on self-rescue and escaping peril!

在野外陌生的环境下，如果缺少司南等指示方向的工具，很容易迷失方向。不过不必担心，我们有很多方法可以帮助你重新找回方向。不过要注意，在寻找方向的过程中请用石子、树枝等物品做好路标，防止原地打转。 
 
方法一：观察天体。白天可以通过观察太阳的位置来辨别方位，太阳在东方升起在西方落下，根据季节的变化可能会有轻微偏移。夜晚则可以观察月亮或北极星的位置辨别。观察日月变相还可以观测时间变化，以便天黑之前回到栖身之所。熟识星象的规律也是一种很重要的辨明方向的方法。 
 
但这种方法有着很大局限性。在一些特殊环境下我们并不能观察到天体进而判断方向，比如阴雨天，或者处于深山密林等遮蔽性较强的空间。 
 
方法二：根据身边的环境来判断方位。比如，如果你发现附近有云根晶矿，你可以将少量云丝放置在晶矿上，云丝会自动聚集到通天塔的方向。其次，稷下的整体地势是西高东低，可以站在高处观察附近的地形，如果有明显的山势起伏和错落的地带则很容易辨别东西方向。如果处在较为低矮的河谷平原地区可以观察河流流向，受地形影响稷下大多数水流的流向是自西向东，也可以根据这一点来大致判断方向。 
 
方法三：通过动植物的特性来判断方向。比如，可以通过观察植物生长的朝向来判断方向，如爪荀果等植物的花朵、果实通常朝南生长。也可以观察果实颜色，朝南一侧的果实颜色更深。若附近恰好有灯华草，可以尝试将其打散，其中的散失的光芒会自动向河流的方向飘去。跟随它找到河流，沿着河流走到平原河谷地带，往往就能找到人口聚居的村镇。 
 
最后，如果处于绝境状态下，请想尽一切办法向外界发送信号，如制造光亮、浓烟、特殊气味等，运气好可能遇到野外探险的风物家和游猎家，不论如何不要放弃自救和脱困！

在野外陌生的环境下，如果缺少司南等指示方向的工具，很容易迷失方向。不过不必担心，我们有很多方法可以帮助你重新找回方向。不过要注意，在寻找方向的过程中请用石子、树枝等物品做好路标，防止原地打转。 
 
方法一：观察天体。白天可以通过观察太阳的位置来辨别方位，太阳在东方升起在西方落下，根据季节的变化可能会有轻微偏移。夜晚则可以观察月亮或北极星的位置辨别。观察日月变相还可以观测时间变化，以便天黑之前回到栖身之所。熟识星象的规律也是一种很重要的辨明方向的方法。 
 
但这种方法有着很大局限性。在一些特殊环境下我们并不能观察到天体进而判断方向，比如阴雨天，或者处于深山密林等遮蔽性较强的空间。 
 
方法二：根据身边的环境来判断方位。比如，如果你发现附近有云根晶矿，你可以将少量云丝放置在晶矿上，云丝会自动聚集到通天塔的方向。其次，稷下的整体地势是西高东低，可以站在高处观察附近的地形，如果有明显的山势起伏和错落的地带则很容易辨别东西方向。如果处在较为低矮的河谷平原地区可以观察河流流向，受地形影响稷下大多数水流的流向是自西向东，也可以根据这一点来大致判断方向。 
 
方法三：通过动植物的特性来判断方向。比如，可以通过观察植物生长的朝向来判断方向，如爪荀果等植物的花朵、果实通常朝南生长。也可以观察果实颜色，朝南一侧的果实颜色更深。若附近恰好有灯华草，可以尝试将其打散，其中的散失的光芒会自动向河流的方向飘去。跟随它找到河流，沿着河流走到平原河谷地带，往往就能找到人口聚居的村镇。 
 
最后，如果处于绝境状态下，请想尽一切办法向外界发送信号，如制造光亮、浓烟、特殊气味等，运气好可能遇到野外探险的风物家和游猎家，不论如何不要放弃自救和脱困！

Month, Date 
 
Today my big brother came back grinning, carrying a long narrow package. He said it had to be a sword inside. I asked him why, and he raised his brows and said, 
 
"Just look at the patina, the sheen—this is an antique!" 
 
But when we opened it, there was only a flute. He was furiously. 
 
He couldn't understand why anyone would give a twig its own box. Maybe he had never seen one before. 
 
 
 
Month, Date 
 
I secretly picked the flute back. My brother tried to snap it a couple of times and couldn't—so the material must be decent. I remembered the neighbors having one when I was little, but I never touched it. After they played, they'd always shake the spit out, and it seemed filthy. 
 
This one looked clean enough. I rinsed it with spring water and left it to dry. 
 
 
 
Month, Date 
 
After two days of trying, I actually got it to sound! But it's a nuisance—you have to shake the spit out after a while. 
 
On my fourth try, I got spit on my brother's face. He didn't say a word, but I could tell he was upset. 
 
 
 
Month, Date 
 
I picked the flute up again. My brother might not be the sharpest, but when it comes to throwing things, he's a pro. 
 
My head still aches from the smack. 
 
Still, I think I'm getting the hang of it. This time it doesn't sound so harsh. 
 
 
 
Month, Date 
 
I've decided to practice in the northern clearing, far enough away not to annoy my brother. 
 
After I swore to keep the flute out of camp, he finally smiled and said if he ever saw it here again, either I or the flute would get snapped in two. 
 
 
 
Month, Date 
 
Bad news: the flute drew in wolves. 
 
Good news: they also brought it back to me. 
 
We ended up playing together for quite a while. 
 
 
 
Month, Date 
 
I realized that if I follow a rhythm, the flute sounds almost pleasant. 
 
Maybe I should buy a songbook in town? 
 
Might need a new flute too—this one's a little bent after brother's rough handling. 
 
But it still plays. I'll keep at it a few more days.

September 25th 
 
I originally planned to stay in Jixia for only a few days, but unexpectedly, I was swamped with work as soon as I arrived. Every day, people come to me for medical consultations or advice, and I have accumulated quite a bit of experience. 
 
The physicians in Jixia are generally called "Herbalists," and they specialize in treating patients with various herbs and potions. They also use a substance called "Aersilk" to assist in healing. Additionally, I have learned that the faction named "Cultivators" among them is the most skilled in researching various novel plants. If I could learn a thing or two, it might give me some new insights.

For generations, the herbalists have roamed mountains and villages—gathering herbs across wilderness, healing ailments among bustling streets—to uphold their creed of compassion in Jixia. 
Since the establishment of the Herb Society, these herbalists have evolved through the seasons, now divided into four distinct schools: Cultivator, innovators who pioneer novel plant cultivation, blending creativity with botanical experimentation. Herbologist, traditionalists preserving ancient wisdom, mastering the knowledge of Jixia's flora across every leaf and root. Healer, pecializing in tonics and healing agents, balancing nourishment and purification. Toxineer, they versed in herbal poisons and animal venoms, wielding danger to neutralize greater threats. 
 
The Cultivators focus on studying and cultivating plants, encouraging students to use their creativity and come up with new and innovative ideas. 
They have improved the quality of herbs, creating many new and improved varieties, each seed in the herb garden is like their child. Under the Cultivators' care, the Herb Garden has become a "herbal reserve" of invaluable herbs for Jixia. 
 
The Herbologists have the longest history among the four factions of the Herbalists. When the Herb Garden was first established, only the Herbologists continued the tradition. 
The students in this faction adhere to tradition and focus on research, aiming to understand every herb and its effects. In addition to historical research, they also conduct systematic analysis, with a very rigorous approach. The traveling Herbologists have a keen eye for spotting the medicinal value of plants and animals. 
 
The tradition of using herbs for health and longevity has been passed down through generations, and the Healers, as a recently established faction, have revived this tradition. 
They are skilled in creating supplements, addressing deficiencies and balancing excesses. The Healers strive for harmony between nature, humanity, and the environment, emphasizing the protection and regulation of the body's healing abilities. They use therapeutic techniques to aid metabolism, maintain balance, and have made medicinal cuisine and nutritional supplements their signature specialties. 
 
The Toxineers, as a unique and innovative faction in the Herb Garden, have a distinct approach, often going against the grain and adhering to the principle that "the right medicine cures the illness." 
They have always been fascinated by toxicology, believing that the judicious use of toxic herbs can have remarkable therapeutic effects. The Toxineers are skilled at identifying the properties of herbs and can develop a wide range of toxins. Rumors circulate that they secretly use their potions to deal with formidable enemies, making them one of the most feared groups in Jixia. 
 
"Prescribe with compassion, use herbs to benefit the people, and heal the world" is the unchanging motto of the Herbalists. Despite the differences between factions, saving lives and alleviating suffering remains the primary duty of all Herbalists.

Contributor: Jixia Countryside Farmer, Guo Rongfu

Content: Complaint regarding the agricultural Mechcrafts provided by the School of Mechcrafts

Editor's Note: Inventions and creations should not disregard reality; they must align with actual life.

Gentlemen of the School of Mechcrafts,

Disturbing you! 

A few days ago when your children delivered that giant Mechanoid, our whole village started using it quickly! The children are lively and enthusiastic, and so is the giant Mechanoid. We got along quite well! However, I also remember the children specifically reminded us this was still an experimental product, urging us to pay close attention and report any issues immediately.

Old Li said that giant Mechanoid was utterly obedient. With just a little oil fed to it, it could transplant an entire village's worth of seedlings neatly, even pulling out all the weeds in the process. Old Li's wife has bad legs, and bending for too long causes severe back pain. Since the giant Mechanoid arrived, her back ailment hasn't flared up again. She insisted I must convey her message, saying the School of Mechcrafts' things are excellent, truly excellent!

However, what I'm about to say probably won't be as pleasing. That giant Mechanoid is indeed hardworking, we villagers all see it. But for some reason, it seems incapable of stopping. Even after all the seedlings were transplanted, it kept pacing back and forth in the fields. While it didn't trample any sprouts, all the fish and shrimp we keep in the fields suffered terribly. And then there's the weeding function. At the time, watching it pull weeds one by one, we thought this reliable lump of iron was quite earnest, deserving maintenance from the village's most experienced blacksmith. Who could have known it only seems able to distinguish seedlings? All other green leaves it categorically considers weeds! Really, what kind of logic is that? Old Zhang in the east village has several plots. Since they're unsuitable for rice, he cultivated a small vegetable garden, sharing the harvest with the whole village. And just like that, in the time it took to sleep, the entire garden was stripped bare!

Old Zhang, furious, insisted on going into the field to reason with the giant Mechanoid. His wife and children together couldn't stop him. But how could that lump of metal understand our rough country talk? The old man poked its round, plump belly with his cane, apparently triggering some prohibition. The giant Mechanoid kept chanting "obstructing work, obstructing work" while shoving Old Zhang, sending him tumbling headfirst into a muddy pit! Those children mentioned earlier it has some defense functions, could guard the village at night. If that's how it guards, forget burglars not daring to come, even we wouldn't dare go out!
Stay tuned for more Jixia Secrets updates.

The new schematic is finished. The problems you pointed out last time were spot on; Shye agrees—it's basically an ignition Mechcraft and doesn't need overengineering. January 22 
 
Li Bai came again today. It's rare to have such a refined customer. I offered him a jar of brew and explained my concerns. 
 
My family has been selling brews in Dreamweave Plains for generations, and customers appreciate the taste. If I make changes recklessly, it might cause problems. Besides, this recipe is the most important thing my father left me. How can I alter it casually? 
 
Li Bai seemed about to say something but stopped, simply smiling and saying, "Well, well. Forget it, let's not talk about that." Then he pulled me into a drinking session. He shared his experiences from various places while drinking, and I discussed my insights into brewing. As we drank and chatted, I fell asleep. 
 
When I woke up, there was no sign of Li Bai, only money scattered on the table and a pair of empty ceramic cups.

A young Herbalist once lost his way in the wilderness. Amid the tangle of weeds, he found only an old man bent over the soil, tilling with quiet persistence. 
 
Sweat trickled down the elder's brow. The boy offered him a flask of water and a cloth to wipe his face. 
 
The old man asked, "Do you know what once grew here?" 
 
Stroking his beard, he began to tell the story: this had once been the plantation of the Herbologists. Countless rare herbs and ancient blossoms had sprung from this barren land. He spoke with reverence of the harvests born of the soil, of the ripening wisdom drawn from age itself. 
 
But the boy replied, "Everything that once blossomed here has already fallen to the ground. What our Cultivators care about are the new sprouts that will grow from this land." 
 
The elder laughed. "New sprouts will one day bear fruit and fall again. Your pursuit is no different from ours in the end." 
 
The boy shook his head. "On the path from sprout to fruit, who can say what may happen?" 
 
If the outcome means nothing, why let life begin? 
 
If growth means nothing, how does one face the days before the fruit is ripe? 
 
They fell silent, unable to answer each other. 
 
As dusk gathered, they finally turned to leave—one old, one young, their silhouettes stretching apart across the wilderness. 
 
Then, at the same moment, their voices rang out: 
 
"A new sprout has taken root here!" 
"A lost fruit still remains here!" 
 
Neither could see the other through the tall grass, yet both wore the same faint, peaceful smile.

As a child, I always looked forward to the warmth of candlelight at night. My grandmother would tuck me in, her voice raspy yet tender as she told me stories. 
She would speak of mountains, rivers, seas, and strange tales. Once, she told me the story of our village. My grandmother and the villagers had spent their lives working on the fertile land, and I had always believed their days were peaceful, in harmony with the seasons. 
But that night, she told me something new. 
My grandmother and the villagers were not the indigenous people here. They had been refugees, displaced by war, wandering in search of a new home until they found this haven. 
As a child, I didn't grasp the hardships hidden in her words, and I didn't like the story. But that night, for the first time, I couldn't sleep. The sorrow in my grandmother's eyes, something even the warm candlelight couldn't soften, haunted me. 
As I grew older, I began to collect stories from the past. Many of the elders who had lived through those events were frail, and I would sit by the window, listening to them recount the history of this land. 
For farmers, nothing is more devastating than watching their fields wither. The villagers left the land they had tended for years because of war. The fires of conflict consumed their crops, and the flames reflected the sadness in their eyes. The land they had worked so hard to cultivate was reduced to ashes, and it could no longer support their hopes. 
My grandmother said that, as farmers, they had lost all hope during those days. 
Unable to survive on barren soil, they packed what little they had and left. Their homes were already in ruins. Each person gathered what they could and set off into uncertainty. 
I was deeply moved by their stories of war, even though I didn't yet realize how much they would shape my own future. 
After my grandmother passed away, many of the other elders who had lived through those times also left. 
By the time I was old enough to travel on my own, there was no one left in the village to tell me those stories. When I shared them with my peers and the children, some were moved, while others said it had nothing to do with them or accused me of exaggerating. 
I didn't mind their indifference, but I knew these stories needed to be passed down. 
So, I set out to gather more stories of war, continuing the journey my grandmother couldn't complete. I will carry on her mission to record the true history, to ensure more people know what happened and remember the sacrifices of our ancestors. 
The peace we enjoy today was built on their sacrifices, and it should never be forgotten.

The supplement to the Saepes Compendium, authored by a Jixia Hunter, documents how to communicate with the Saepes. 
Though territorial and often hostile to outsiders, it is possible to communicate with them—especially the smaller ones. 
Firstly, small Saepes understand basic body language. Show them your unarmed hands as a sign of peace. Here are some simple gestures: 
1. Cup your cheeks, look up: "Is your sky clear?" Sun-loving Saepes consider this a greeting. 
2. Hands on hips, hop left then right: "How are you today?" If they repeat the action, it means they're happy; if they raise their hands then lower them, they're unhappy. 
3. Claw-like hands over temples, neck stretched out: "I want to go." If they step aside, it's an invitation; if they don't move, take another path. 
Note: There are many more gestures. For further learning, visit me at the academy. Alternatively, if you're too lazy to learn these gestures but still wish to avoid the Saepes camp, try this trick passed down from locals: most small Saepes have a strong urge to clean up litter. Scatter sunflower seeds or beads on the ground, and while they're busy picking them up, stroll past (don't be embarrassed; Saepes enjoy collecting trinkets). 
Another method is using floral language. Certain flowers, fruits, and mushrooms hold special meanings for Saepes. Place these items before them to convey your intentions. Known examples include: 
1. Clanging Grass: Thank you. 
2. Butterfly Flower: Hello. 
3. Illusive Butterfly Flower: Blessings. 
4. Pawpaw: I understand you; here's a hug. 
5. Java Apple: Goodbye. 
Additionally, offering a piece of an Aervein beast claw with palms facing upwards signifies, "We share a common enemy; we're friends." If they accept it, it means they hold no hostility towards you. 
Beware: there is one item you should never show a Saepes—namely, Imbued Twigs, sheddings from plant-based creatures, mostly from defeated Saepes. Displaying Imbued Twigs to a Saepes is considered a declaration of war, and they will fight you to the death. 
Comment: I, Mu Ping, the Hunter most familiar with Saepes, am currently developing a third approach: crafting realistic costumes from natural bark and leaves collected painstakingly from the ground! Theoretically, wearing such attire could allow perfect integration into Saepes society for close observation. Although the first prototype's field test results were less than ideal, I remain confident! 
Comment (Herbalist): To readers, after Mu Ping's first field test in costume, he used up half a year's worth of my topical ointments just to recover. Please exercise caution. 
Regardless of which method you choose, sincerity is key when communicating with Saepes. Don't assume they're mindless beings; in fact, Saepes can discern genuine intent from subtle body movements. When encountering someone who truly wishes to befriend them, small Saepes may even bloom a single flower atop their head. 
According to ancient Jixia legends, this flower grows from a Saepes' life force, its heart. Only those with pure souls and no ill intentions can make a Saepes bloom, and that person will carry the flower forever. As their time nears its end, Saepes return to their human friend's home under the cover of night, leaving the flower upon the doorway before quietly departing. 
If their human companion has already passed away, Saepes place the flower where their friend was laid to rest. Miraculously, they always find the right spot. 
While only a legend, it remains a touching tale.

The Societies are spread far and wide across Jixia, and even beyond its borders; their presence can still be felt. Each Society pursues its own studies with unshakable passion and dedication; some of its research topics take generations to show the slightest progress. In the spirit of fairness, I've conducted interviews with various individuals across Jixia. Below are excerpts from those conversations. 
 
Interviewee: Administrator of the Mission Board 
Location: Frostcloud Town 
 
Q: What do you think of the Societies? 
A: The Societies? They're the most restless bunch around! Always stirring up trouble for everyone. 
Q: Do they often give you problems? 
A: Not exactly, more like they keep posting bizarre commissions on my board. Like, an Intelligencer who's terrible at public speaking looking for someone to argue on their behalf in Frostcloud Town; a rookie Hunter asking people to capture eighteen different species around the Aerfall Highlands; an Herbalist student seeking brave volunteers to test the toxicity of strange plants in the northern Dreamscape... It's endless. There's nothing too odd for them to attempt. 
Q: Do people ever actually take on those requests? 
A: Hardly ever, but sometimes they get lucky. 
Q: Then maybe I should post one myself. Who knows, maybe someone will take over my fieldwork for me... 
 
Interviewee: A respected Seeker 
Location: Western camp, Aerfall Highlands 
 
Q: As a Seeker, do you get along well with members of other Societies? 
A: Get along? Ha! Everyone sticks to their own ways. If we can talk for ten minutes without arguing, that's already a miracle! 
Q: So... you don't have a good relationship with them? 
A: No, no, it's not like that. We bicker, sure, sometimes even get jealous of one another. But when it comes to helping each other in a pinch, no one hesitates. 
Q: Oh? So you mean you may quarrel, but deep down you're united? 
A: Let me tell you something. Last year, I discovered ruins that seemed related to dragons. Couldn't find the Dragonologist who might know more. Then an Intelligencer caught wind of it, spread the word, and helped us gather information. We followed their leads deep into the wilderness and got completely lost. Luckily, a Hunter out there guided us back on track, and a Gourmet kept us fed so we could keep going. Eventually, we reached a valley, only for the rain to pour for days. It was a solitary Angler who led us to shelter, a cave nearby. 
When the rain finally stopped, a Musician who was traveling with us began to play a melody. And guess what? The very Dragonologist we'd been searching for heard the music, mistook it for a dragon's call, and appeared out of nowhere! You should've seen how thrilled we all were. 
Q: So, did you ever solve the mystery of the ruins? 
A: Not at all! We were so excited that we spent the whole night talking, heart to heart, with the Musician playing beside us. By dawn, we'd completely forgotten what we came for, ha!

text: Honestly, I'm deeply disappointed with the School of Mechcraft and Jixia's current approach to studying and developing Mechanoids. I used to respect their ingenuity, but why squander so much effort on making them "practical for daily life"? That kind of thinking is superficial—it shows no respect at all for what Mechcrafts truly are. The true purpose of Mechcraft lies in surpassing the limits of the human body and tools—in battle. To reduce them to household conveniences is to belittle their potential! They fail to see the infinite possibilities of Mechcrafts in combat; they can't grasp the true romance of what Mechcrafts represent. I refuse to lose myself in the small comforts they offer. I will give Mechcrafts their true transformation—let them realize their real purpose in the crucible of battle.

After days of travel, I finally arrived at Jixia Academy. 
 
 
 
My weary body reminded me of the arduous journey. I've traveled to many places, but few rival the winding mountain paths of Jixia. 
 
The mountains stretched endlessly, each peak leading to the next, while streams murmured through lush green valleys. One wrong turn, and you could easily lose your way in this charming wilderness. 
 
 
 
Jixia Academy sits atop the highest peak of Jixia Mountain, offering a breathtaking view of the landscape through wisps of cloud: the verdant Springbrook Plains, the fertile Harvest Fields, and the majestic Aerfall Highlands. 
 
 
 
As I gazed at the paths I had traversed, I marveled at how the mountains, which had taken days to climb, now seemed no bigger than autumn leaves, with the people below mere invisible specks busy with their lives. In that moment, I couldn't decide whether to marvel at nature's grandeur or reflect on the insignificance of mankind. 
 
 
 
Jixia Academy, the pinnacle of education in Jixia, was the destination of my long journey. 
 
I explored the campus, taking in the lively Martial Arts classes, the elegant Sorcery Runes, the intricate Mechcrafts, and the magnificent Wonders. 
 
 
 
My visit, however, wasn't without incident. Exhausted from days of hiking, I had to admit my fatigue. The teachers hosting me suggested I rest for a day or two before continuing my tour. 
 
 
 
I was truly grateful for their generosity. They called in a group of students, Herbalists, as I later learned, skilled in treating all kinds of ailments. The balms they provided worked wonders. After a few days of rest in the dorms they arranged for me, I felt rejuvenated—almost reborn. 
 
 
 
The mountains, seas, and clouds of Jixia are rare sights in this world, but what struck me as truly extraordinary were the passionate people of Jixia Academy. Even long after I leave Jixia, their faces will remain vivid in my mind. And whenever that happens, I'll cast aside my doubts and prepare to scale the next mountain peak I face.

In ancient times there was a great bear whose breath roared like thunder, and people hailed it as an omen of blessing. But when illness struck the beast, the villagers sought help from a healer. 
 
A man with golden hair appeared and led the bear away. Long after, he returned, and the beast's wounds were healed. The people rejoiced—until strange markings appeared upon the bear's body. 
 
That night the creature turned violent, mauling many without restraint. The villagers, stricken with fear, subdued it and sealed it with a talisman. 
 
All knew it was a spirit beast, and none dared to kill it. Instead they left a charge to those who came after: seek the truth hidden in those markings. And if the creature once more brings harm, then release it swiftly from its suffering.

Thank you, reader, for making it through all the rambling bits of fishing lore in these pages. As this series comes to a close, there's one last question I'd like to leave with you: What is the true purpose of fishing? 
 
 
 
For some, it's a way to cultivate the self. The Riverreads see it as a discipline of character—sitting motionless for hours, turning inward, reflecting on the ways of the world. They care little for how many fish are caught, content with the old saying: those who wish to bite, will bite. The Stillminds, on the other hand, seek solitude. They cast their lines in quiet, secluded spots, savoring the sense of connection between rod, stream, fish, and the greater whole of nature. 
 
 
 
Others, the Gearheads, prize results. To them, the catch is both proof of skill and a goal in itself. They host competitions across Jixia, vying to see who can claim the title of master angler. And then there are the gluttons of the trade, whose joy lies in cooking and eating; their eyes are always on the quantity of the catch. 
 
 
 
I remember, three years ago at an angling tournament, someone asked me: "Don't you think that chasing only results and victory is a little...less noble? Not dishonorable, exactly, but compared to those who seek meaning in the act itself, aren't we...you know." I brushed it off at the time, without giving a real answer. Truthfully, I hadn't sorted out the matter of fishing for the catch versus fishing for the act. 
 
 
 
Now, though, I think there is no final answer. Both sides are right—those who prize the process, and those who prize the outcome. You are not a fish, how can you know the fish's joy? We cannot speak for others, nor truly feel what they gain from their time by the water. We can only tend to ourselves—relishing every cast, every moment of uncertainty, every surge of excitement when the line goes taut. As the saying goes: "For the one who fishes, it is enough to be at peace with one's own heart—do your part, and leave the rest to fate."

You still don't get it, do you? Father chose me, not you! 
 
 
 
The person angrily shouting in front of me was my half-brother, Zhou Yann. Right behind him was my stepmother, clearly here to back him up. 
 
They were here again, trying to convince me to give up my claim to our family's Mechcraft legacy. Just like the last few times, my brother wore that same smug expression — as if he'd swallowed a whole Flameroll Fruit. 
 
 
 
"Zhou Ying, I think it's time you faced reality," Zhou Yann sneered, pulling something out of his bag and tossing it onto the wooden table. 
 
"This is a letter from Father. Take a good look." 
 
 
 
A letter from Father? My heart sank as I opened it, carefully examining every detail, wary of any forgery. 
 
But the handwriting, the tone — it was undeniably his. 
 
 
 
The letter started with some concern for my well-being, a few words about the family, and then suddenly shifted: 
 
"My daughter, there's something I've been considering for a while, and your mother often brings it up too. I'm planning to bring you back to Chang'an from Jixia. Once you're home, I won't force you to study Mechcraft anymore. You can do whatever you like, just as you wish. 
 
Your mother is right — I've been too hard on you. It wasn't my intention, but I can't take our family's legacy lightly, and your last few exam results... To be honest, they've been quite disappointing. 
 
Here's what we'll do: I hear the next Mechcraft exam is coming up soon. I'll return to see how you both perform. If you're still the same as before, I'll have no choice but to leave your brother in Jixia to continue his studies alone. Take care of yourself..." 
 
 
 
Cold sweat soaked through my clothes, and the letter trembled in my hands. 
 
"So, do you understand now? You've already lost," Zhou Yann said smugly. 
 
"Lost? Not necessarily. Father said he would consider the next Mechcraft exam results before—" I started to argue, but someone cut me off. 
 
 
 
"With your bottom-rank Mechcraft scores, can anything you build even function?" My stepmother finally spoke up, her tone dripping with disdain. If Zhou Yann had swallowed one Flameroll Fruit, she must have downed three, and rotten ones at that. 
 
 
 
"Do you really think you're qualified?" Zhou Yann jeered. "I suggest you pack up and head back to Chang'an yourself, before you embarrass yourself in front of Father." 
 
 
 
My stepmother chimed in, "Exactly. You're just wasting time here. Why not go back home and make room for someone who's actually serious?" 
 
 
 
"No way," I snapped. "I'm not giving up just like that. I'll give it my all in the next Mechcraft exam. If you think I'm going to quit so easily, you can forget about it!" 
 
 
 
"You... you're..." Zhou Yann was trembling with anger. 
 
"Enough, why waste energy on someone like her? Calm down, no need to get worked up. Let's go. We'll see who ends up embarrassed," my stepmother said, pulling Zhou Yann away. 
 
He shot me one last furious glance before they left, repeatedly looking back as they walked away. 
 
 
 
The world grew quiet, but my mind was anything but at peace. 
 
To be honest, after coming to Jixia, being away from my family's control, I had gotten a bit too reckless. Skipping classes, getting lost in fishing, failing to live up to my father's expectations, and making little progress in Mechcraft... 
 
 
 
But, can I really give up just like that? I admit I've been lazy and haven't worked hard enough, but if you think I'm going to surrender so easily, especially to those two, it's not happening. No way. I won't let that happen. Even if there's only a slim chance, I'm going to take it!

I explained that Ice Fruit makes dishes too cold and advised him to balance the flavor with some chili oil. He thanked me, saying his friends would enjoy the meal.

Did Kongming really serve this fish to Zhou Yu? No wonder Zhou Yu looked so terrible around that time. Looking back, it's quite embarrassing.

As the foremost educational institution in Aercocoon, Jixia Academy holds significant sway over the education and employment of young people. However, after an in-depth investigation, it has come to my attention that the state of its students is cause for concern. 
 
 
 
The School of Martial Arts fosters a crowd of hot-headed, violence-prone fanatics. 
These students gorge on food and are obsessed with competition and battle, recklessly pursuing victory and showcasing their strength. This leads them down a path of excessive rivalry and conflict, trapping them in a cycle of violence. This behavior will undoubtedly have severe negative impacts on their personal growth and social harmony. 
 
 
 
In contrast, the School of Sorcery breeds silent, cold-blooded monsters. 
These individuals often exhibit indifference and a lack of emotional expression. They are emotionally repressed, sensitive, and overly critical, priding themselves on being above worldly concerns. Their mental health is severely impaired, likely causing distress to those around them. 
 
 
 
Lastly, there are the curious, nosy busybodies from the School of Mechcraft, who are driven by gossip and pointless questions. 
Their sole interest lies in novelty, even if it means breaking taboos and boundaries to study so-called "mechanical arts." At best, they waste effort creating useless scrap; at worst, they generate dangerous constructs with no redeeming value. 
 
 
 
No wonder the esteemed Jixia Academy would obstruct our humble workshop publications at every turn—they fear these secrets spilling out, like dark clouds dreading the dispersal by sunlight.

When I visited the School of Mechcrafts to commission climbing Mechcrafts, I learned about a student renowned for his knowledge of ancient warfare. But when I tried to engage him in conversation, I was turned away. As I asked around, I realized this student's past was more compelling than any war story. 
 
 
 
He was indeed highly knowledgeable about various legends and past wars, often sharing these stories with his classmates. However, he held most modern Mechcrafts in contempt, often criticizing his peers' work as overly complex failures. 
 
 
 
He longed for the legendary ancient Mechcrafts—simple, practical designs with unparalleled destructive power. 
 
 
 
He fantasized that one day, when war returned, he would rise like the legendary heroes, achieving great feats with his inventions. 
 
 
 
One day, as usual, he criticized a classmate's Mechcraft. Tired of his constant critiques, the student finally shot back: "Here we go again. Are you going to tell us another story about giant bronze Mechdroids fighting monsters?" The crowd burst into laughter. 
 
 
 
"You! Just you wait, I will definitely..." He was about to explode in anger but realized everyone had already walked away. 
 
 
 
"I will find true ancient Mechcrafts and prove your ignorance!" he muttered to himself, with no one there to hear. 
 
 
 
Early the next morning, he went to Master Mozi to ask for leave, determined to find real ancient Mechcrafts. Instead of talking him out of it, Master Mozi gave him the locations of ancient war ruins and some precautions. 
 
 
 
The student was so excited he could barely sleep that night. Tomorrow, he thought, tomorrow I will finally see the magnificent ancient Mechcrafts—bronze beasts covered in intricate patterns, ingenious weapons, and so much more... 
At the first light of dawn, he set out. With Mozi's directions in hand, the student arrived at his destination without much trouble. 
 
 
 
But what greeted him were remnants of armor and weapons scattered across the ground, dilapidated bronze Mechcrafts, unburied skeletal remains, and weeds growing everywhere... 
 
 
 
It was nothing like he had imagined—bleak, oppressive. Words failed him as he tried to speak. As he wandered through the valley, the howling wind carried his thoughts away. 
 
 
 
He imagined himself on that ancient battlefield, standing armed with weapons, as arrows whizzed by and shells exploded around him. Giant bronze Mechcrafts charged through the fray amidst the relentless cacophony of combat and senseless shouts. 
 
 
 
Or maybe, he was the inventor of these Mechcrafts, having crafted the most formidable devices the world had ever known. But to what end? Slaughter, destruction, annihilation. These extraordinary inventions had been twisted against the very civilization that created them, obliterating everything in their path. How had things come to this? 
 
 
 
It was a cool autumn day, with gusts of mountain wind sweeping through. There, the bewildered student stood alone, his clothes drenched in sweat... 
 
 
 
According to his friends, after returning from the ruins, he seemed like a different person—silent and often lost in thought, muttering to himself. The confident talks that once defined him had vanished. 
 
 
 
Sometimes, he would ask profound questions, like "What is the purpose of studying and inventing Mechcrafts?" and "Why did the ancients use such advanced inventions to slaughter one another?" Recently, he had been visiting the Master more frequently, saying there was still much to learn. 
 
 
 
"Just yesterday, he said the war ruins had taught him the most valuable lesson of his life. He even asked who wanted to accompany him on a return trip," his friend said. "Haha, it seems like this time he's planning to be our teacher."

Another all-nighter. I finally finished preparing for my afternoon class. Just as I lay down to rest, there was a sudden knock at the door. 
 
"It's me, Xiaotong," a voice called from outside. 
"The door's unlocked. Come on in." I replied, too exhausted to get up. 
The door burst open, and someone slipped inside, sliding all the way to my bedside and plopping down onto it. 
"Zhou Ying, still in bed? Let's go fishing. You haven't come in almost a month. You're always so busy studying. It's not good to be so stressed out all the time. You need to find a balance," Xiaotong said with a smile, pulling on my hand. 
"I've just lain down." 
"You... you stayed up all night again? Oh dear, can your body take this? Your grades have been good lately. Many instructors have praised your progress. Don't push yourself too hard." 
"My grades aren't good enough yet. And I need to prepare for the next Mechcraft test. I must not let my stepmother and brother succeed, and I cannot disappoint my father." 
"Yes, them again. Your family situation is really complicated." 
Xiaotong blinked her big, shining eyes and looked around the room until she spotted a Mechcraft on the table. 
"What's that? A six-joint tenon? Didn't know you still played with toys like that." 
"It just looks that way... It's actually a new kind of tenon-and-mortise lock Mechcraft I'm designing. With just one strong press, it can make the Mechanoid fall apart in an instant." 
"Fall apart? What's the point of that?" 
"Well, it makes adjustments easier, of course! Once this structure is complete, repairing Mechanoids won't require all that tedious disassembly. But I'm not done yet—after my nap, I'll keep working." 
"What? You have more work to do? Then I won't disturb you—I wouldn't want to rob you of your precious sleep time." She got ready to leave. 
"Alright then, see you later... Oh, and please close the door gently..." 
 
CLUNK—Too late. 
 
This went on for another two weeks. Finally, the theme for the Mechcraft exam was announced: a small-scale Mechanoid duel. 
 
I worked day and night for a week and finished my design. Now, all I had to do was put everything together. 
 
I breathed a sigh of relief. There were five days left before the exam, and even if it took me three full days to finish everything, I'd still have plenty of time. 
 
"Why don't we relax at Upstream Camp? I feel like I'm growing moss here." I thought to myself, tidied up my room, quickly cleaned myself up, and pushed open the door. 
 
In Jixia, the early autumn air still held the warmth of summer. The sun shone down, cozy but also signaling the prelude to the next season, as the north wind blew, refreshing the mind and spirit. 
 
The comfortable weather relaxed my tense nerves, letting me forget my worries for a while and simply enjoy the connection between my body and nature. But before I could savor this feeling any longer, it was shattered by a voice. 
 
"Zhou Ying? Why are you here?" 
I turned my head toward the sound, and it was my stepmother again. 
I ignored her, but she walked quickly toward me. 
"Why? Still mad at me?" My stepmother asked with a forced smile, walking closer. "You didn't listen when I explained things before. I was only trying to help." 
"Thanks." 
"Don't take it so hard." She paused before continuing, "Look, I know I favor Yaan sometimes, but deep down, you're both my children. I love you both equally." 
"Just say what you mean," I said, annoyed. I didn't want to hear her excuses. 
"Fine, I will. If you drop out of this competition, once Yaan inherits our family's Mechcraft techniques, he can teach you. That sounds fair, right? I think your father would agree." 
"Thank you for your kindness. If I win, I might consider teaching him." 
"You..." My stepmother's face twitched in anger. 
 
"Do you really think you can convince me with these tricks?" I glared at her. "Enough. Let Zhou Yaan and me compete fairly!" 
"Don't regret this." She dropped that line and left without looking back. 
 
My stepmother ruined my good mood. Ugh, I should just go back and keep working on my designs... 
 
Back in my dorm, I collapsed into a chair, staring blankly at the workbench, but something felt off. 
 
Suddenly, I realized something was wrong! Maybe I was too tired, but it took me a while to realize—the design was gone. 
 
I tore the whole room apart but found no trace of it... 
 
Could they have snuck in and stolen it while I was out? Dammit! 
 
Only five days left until the exam. What am I going to do now?

Master Piner spoke nonstop between sips of tea. 
 
I had always been curious about him. As a rather famous Mechcraft master, his booming voice and unbroken enthusiasm almost outshone his Mechcraft skill. His conversation flowed endlessly, and I often struggled to keep pace. 
 
A few days ago, I received an invitation from this very Piner, an old friend of Mr. Luban, to visit him at the Honor Tower in the Iridescent Basin. 
 
Honor Tower stands as the basin's highest point, an unrivaled place for viewing the clouds and peaks. Ever the gracious host, Master Piner had prepared an impressive spread of teas and delicacies. 
 
I'd heard about him before coming, his warmth, his talkativeness, and how he once participated in the Enlightenment Trials during his student days. Though he couldn't participate in his final year due to unknown reasons, his remarkable knowledge of Mechcraft earned him a teaching position, and now he oversees the Honor Tower itself. 
 
I had yet to witness his famed craftsmanship firsthand, but his gift of speech alone was a marvel. Our tea gathering stretched from sunrise to sunset without pause, and still, he hardly drew breath. 
 
At last, near evening, a student arrived with a question, interrupting the flow of words. I took the chance to excuse myself and step out to the balcony for air. 
 
A gentle breeze rose, carrying thin mist through the valley. The vapor drifted upward, touching the sky like a silver thread drawn from the clouds. 
The mountains were half-veiled, the treetops swayed, and the cool air washed over me with a sense of quiet renewal. 
 
 
Below, the students in Dainty Vale had stopped their training, laughing and pointing toward the deepening mist. I too stood watching, lost in the dreamlike beauty of the scene. 
 
The evening fog rides the wind, drifting into memory; old dreams fade where the iridescent clouds return. 
 
Perhaps life itself is like this, each of us swept along by fate, yet still finding our own moments of brilliance. 
 
I turned back toward Master Piner. The tea was steaming again, the lamps relit, and the room alive once more with chatter. Soon, an Angler arrived with a great fish, followed by a Hunter carrying fresh game. The Gourmets on the tower prepared a feast, and our gathering turned lively once again. Until, before we knew it, dawn had come.

Every day I write about my life and feelings, but it feels meaningless.

Freedom, creativity, and independence are wonderful, yet I'm now trapped by the world's rules and can't fight them. Breaking those rules could bring unpredictable consequences—I might lose everything—but I can't accept living like this. 
 
I want to live, write, and create honestly, true to myself. To find real happiness, I need to find who I really am. 
 
I hope someone will discover the secrets hidden in my writings. Please—I have no other options.

Before I began writing in earnest, I often wavered. Could I really produce a book worth passing down, or would I labor for years only to fail, ending in quiet regret? 
 
 
 
One day, while I sat in gloom, a young village girl came to visit, and I learned her story. 
 
 
 
Her favorite place was the smithy—the warm glow of the furnace, the rhythm of hammer on metal. Each time she tried to touch the tools, her uncle scolded her. 
 
 
 
The craftsmen never let her inside, so she stole scraps of iron and wood to practice in secret. Her brother mocked her, saying a girl had no business with weapons or forging, that it was all wasted effort. 
 
 
 
The thought that all the smiths might feel the same cut her deeply. She climbed a tree near the workshop, watching the busy men at work, and wept. 
 
 
 
An old man found her there. 
 
 
 
He laughed and said, "So it's you making the rain." 
 
 
 
He caught her as she jumped down, listened to her troubles, and stroked his beard. 
 
 
 
His beard was long, and when he laughed it brushed against her cheek, tickling her. 
 
 
 
Then he told her a story. Long ago, in a time of war, the villagers were driven from their homes. On the road they met bears taller than trees and lizards that could swallow a man whole. The farmers were helpless—until one woman stepped forward. 
 
 
 
Night after night she stood guard, fighting off monsters and foes. 
 
 
 
You would think that she was some kind of prodigy. 
 
 
 
Yet, at the start of the war she had never held a weapon; the villagers thought her efforts foolish. But she said she was only following her heart. Whatever the outcome, she would not allow herself to live in disappointment. 
 
 
 
In times of turmoil no one could escape the whirlpool, no matter their station. Villages burned, families scattered—but her blade became their shelter. 
 
 
 
She honed her skills, forged her own path of Martial Arts, and in the end protected her people. In the vast ocean of martial traditions, her insights might have seemed ordinary.  
 
 
 
But they saved countless lives. People remembered her with gratitude and reverence. To them she was a hero; to herself, she had already become one long before. 
 
 
 
The old man said: once your heart is set, do not fear other voices. Identity, gender, age—these are only trifles beside a steadfast will. Wherever you are, if you keep faith and persist, your efforts will one day bear fruit. 
 
 
 
And by then, no matter what others say, you will already be a true hero. 
 
 
 
The girl wiped her tears, looked at the new calluses on her hands, and clenched them tightly. 
 
 
 
Two years later, through hard training, she earned permission to work as an apprentice in the smithy. When she told me this story, with a gravity far beyond her years, I couldn't help but smile. 
 
 
 
The voice of that war-born heroine still echoes through time—she inspired the child's growth, and now steels my own resolve. Where the heart points, strength will follow; and in time, an answer will come. 
 
 
 
Even in the darkest days, there are those who listen to the call within and become heroes—first to themselves, and then to others. Against such light, my own small doubts seem hardly worth mentioning. 
 
 
 
And so, in tracing the scars of war, I may yet bring to others the memory of human courage that shone even in its cruelest hours.

Sea and sky merge into one; the ocean is deep blue, with sunlight and waves reflecting off each other as the surf crashes against the sea-coral rocks. This is the border of Jixia—the Sea Realm—and also my last stop before leaving Jixia. 
 
A new friend at the academy told me that the rivers of Jixia are strange and varied, and if I didn't witness these wonders, I would miss the essence of Jixia. I took his word for it, hired a boat to go downstream, and waited in anticipation for the wonders along the way. 
 
The boatman remembered me as a passenger at first, but when a fiery red giant fish leaped out of the water, he forgot I was still on board and rowed hard to chase after it. 
"The Fish King! You don't see this guy even a few times a year!" he exclaimed excitedly to himself. After several hours of pursuit, the boatman lost the rare Fish King, and I ended up in the Sea Realm Rocklands, far from my destination, Baiming Port. 
 
The boatman felt a bit apologetic and said he intended to compensate me with fish. I declined, and instead, in high spirits, asked him to take me on a tour of the Sea Realm Rocklands. It was worth it to have ancient legends accompany the clear river water as they brought me to the seaside. 
 
Two days later, the small boat docked slowly at Baiming Port. I stepped onto the pier and silently bid farewell to the Tongtian Tower in my heart. The unique clouds in the sky silently displayed the appearance of Jixia. The clouds were sometimes like small streams of early spring, sometimes like slow-moving giant beasts, and water vapor steamed from the sea as the clouds grew thicker. Between the clouds and the sky, a behemoth seemed to be hidden, swimming among them. Its broad body looked like a giant fish, or perhaps a roc. 
 
I couldn't help but recall the rumors I heard in Zhulang Village in the Sea Realm Rocklands about people seeing the Kun swimming in the ocean east of Jixia. Could it really be the Kun? 
Locals say that seeing the Kun is a good omen that can change one's luck or bring unexpected gifts. For me, the scenery I witnessed in Jixia and the people I met were already proof of my good fortune. 
I shouted my thanks to the Kun in the sky, drawing puzzled looks from the crowd, who asked who I was talking to. 
 
"I believe the legends are true."

Deep within the library of Jixia Academy lies a little-known corner, my secret haven as a nameless student.

I knew I was different from the others, not in wisdom, but in my presence so ordinary it bordered on invisibility. Yet, fate loved to play jokes, plunging me into that dazzling world when I least expected it.

Senior Yango, a legend of Jixia Academy, possessed puppetry skills that left onlookers in awe, with every move drawing countless eyes. For me, he was the hand that reached out in times of need, a shadow that kept me company in loneliness.

Now, looking at myself, I couldn't help but pinch my arm in disbelief.

This body wasn't sensitive to pain, but the genuine sensation told me I had indeed become a puppet.

What should I do...? Just as I was trying to figure out an escape, I saw Senior Yango standing at the door.

"What's wrong, little puppet?" asked the handsome puppet beside him with a smiling voice.

I glanced over, and a hint of amusement also flashed across Senior Yango's face. I had never closely observed him before, and only now did I realize his striking beauty. The sharply defined edges of his face, the captivating smile at the corners of his lips, and those star-like, slender eyes gleamed with a cool light under his black eyebrows.

My heart trembled, leaving me standing there speechless. But the senior approached unaware, his hand gently touching my face, and even the puppet's tone softened, "Little puppet, are you malfunctioning?"

If I still had a human face, I would have blushed to the ears. But amidst the nervousness, I remembered that pretending to be a broken puppet might be the best solution.

"Yes... something seems wrong," I said, my eyes wandering as I lied.

Fortunately, Senior Yango didn't suspect anything. He lightly patted my head and reassured me, "Don't worry, we'll check it out."

After examining me, Senior Yango found nothing unusual with this puppet body. Just as I was panicking about how to explain, he smiled and the puppet said, "Maybe you're just feeling cooped up here. Would you like to come out and take a walk with me?"

As expected of Senior Yango, he showed such profound care for his puppets...

I was shocked in my heart but nodded.

This became my favorite day since entering the academy.

The time spent with Senior Yango brought me unprecedented joy. He was assertive yet gentle, and every inspection he performed made me feel his care and protection.

He would take me on moonlit walks at night. The silver light spilled over the puppet body, as if draping me in a mysterious veil.

But my happiness was always short-lived and fleeting.

After traveling with me for half a month, Senior Yango and I returned to the academy.

It was then that I slowly realized I wasn't the only puppet. Besides me, there were other puppets by his side, each with their own unique characteristics.

Whenever Senior Yango controlled them, they radiated dazzling lights, making me feel pressure and unease I'd never known before.

In truth, I remained the most unremarkable one. Watching the senior dance with the other puppets, a bitter loneliness engulfed my beating heart.

-End of Book 1-

After two weeks of traveling outside, I decided it was time to return to the academy to find a way to reclaim my body.

During this time, I searched everywhere for clues, hoping to find a way to restore myself. Eventually, I learned that Master Zhuangzi, known for interpreting dreams, had once solved a similar case of soul displacement.

With both trepidation and anticipation, I visited Master Zhuangzi's residence. After hearing my story, he pondered for a moment before speaking slowly:

"Restoring your body won't be easy. You'll need to find a mysterious herb capable of awakening your soul, and perform the ritual under the full moon. Only then can you regain control of your body."

Overwhelmed with gratitude, I thanked Master Zhuangzi and immediately embarked on a quest for the herb. The journey was arduous, but I pressed on, undaunted. Whenever loneliness crept in, Senior Yango's smile would appear before my eyes. Finally, during the recent full moon, I discovered the herb.

My body lay in the dormitory, mistaken by others for a deep sleep due to an injury. Who could believe that my soul now dwelled within a puppet? I asked Master Zhuangzi to retrieve my body, and under his guidance, we performed the ritual.

As I lay on the stone bed, I gazed upon my sleeping self. My neglected body looked worn, and those who disliked me naturally didn't visit or care for me. I was never a stunning beauty, and now my appearance bordered on ugly. But it didn't matter—I believed I had changed, and things would only improve from here.

I closed my eyes peacefully, feeling a powerful force flow into me. Yet there was no pain—just the sensation of drifting in warm water as my soul gradually merged with my body.

"That's good," a familiar puppet voice whispered softly, almost like an illusion. "No need to tell her I was here."

Was I so homesick for Senior Yango that I imagined his voice? But I couldn't open my eyes.

When I finally regained consciousness, I had returned to my own body. Master Zhuangzi smiled at me, with no one else present.

It must have been my imagination.

I bid farewell to Master Zhuangzi and walked toward the academy, bathed in today's warm sunlight.

End of Book 1

Dreamweave Plains 
A wild and ancient land, home to the settlers of Jixia, and a cradle of countless old legends. 
 
I've temporarily left my caravan to follow an Eastern physician who wanders the continent. He brought me here—to a place called the Dreamweave Plains. "The field where dreams are woven." What a name—so lyrical, so full of Eastern poetry. On the way, his words stirred something deep within me: he believes this is where I might find the miraculous herb that could heal my mother. 
 
We stopped to rest in Harvest Bazaar, where the innkeeper insisted we try the local specialties. Every dish was infused with native herbs—ingredients said to nourish the body before illness can ever take hold. According to Eastern wisdom, gentle nourishment is the best medicine. The flavors were strange but comforting, their warmth spreading from the tongue to the heart. As we ate, the physician told me more about this land. Sheltered by the great Aerux, Harvest Fields are the richest farmlands in all of Jixia. Villages here have thrived since ancient times—fishing, herding, and tilling the soil. Each spring and autumn, students from the academy come to help with planting and harvest. Horses trample the mud, laughter fills the air, and all across the plains you see old and young laboring side by side. When the work is done, they celebrate with the Harvest Festival, ringing a great bell that can be heard across the plains. They paint children's foreheads with bright designs, share festival foods, and give thanks to the cloud silkworms for their year's blessings—praying for fair winds and gentle rain to come. 
 
I asked the physician—who proudly named himself an Herbalist—if the stories of miraculous plants were true. 
 
He smiled and said that the Herb Garden was indeed the seat of their Society. Here, Herbalists from across the East gather to study rare flora and refine medicines. Nearly every plant that can be cultivated in Jixia grows here, nourished by the life-giving flow of Aerux. The land is so fertile that even the air seems to shimmer with vitality. In this single region, he said, one could witness the very pinnacle of Eastern healing arts. My heart leapt at his words. 
 
But then his expression grew somber. He raised a hand to temper my excitement and said something with quiet gravity—a phrase full of that old Eastern philosophy: "Fortune and disaster are born of the same root." The Aerux that blesses these plains does not only nurture life—it awakens it. An ancient, long-dormant plant called the Moonelia Sprout has begun to revive, spreading uncontrollably. Its creeping roots cling to buildings, taint the water, and worse yet, it has begun to merge with the Aerux itself. If left unchecked, it could threaten all of Harvest Fields and even the Cloudreach Tower. And the dangers do not end there. On this thriving land where life flourishes so fiercely, beasts and monsters grow stronger, more aggressive—some plants have even begun to take on living form. Wherever rare and wondrous herbs grow, traces of these creatures soon follow...

Research Finding: 
 
During a rescue of a student bewildered by Oneiros, using frozen Sorcery slightly helped him to clear his mind, and the student temporarily calmed down. 
 
Research Record: 
 
After multiple experiments, it appears that frozen Sorcery can slightly suppress Oneiros and also prevent it from easily dissipating after leaving the Dreamscape. This case requires further research.

It's extremely risky for a dreamer to be unable to awaken from a dream. In the worst case, they might be trapped in the dream indefinitely. Therefore, having someone nearby to help is important. When a dreamer cannot rouse themselves, a companion can use Sorcery Techniques to awaken the dreamer.

Sailing into Jixia 
 
 
 
A winged sailship glides across the sea, a common sight at Baiming Harbor, yet it is the unsung hero that has opened the doors to Jixia. 
 
 
 
Crossing the Springbrook River, you will reach Jixia. The harbor here is as bustling as the river, with countless sailships carrying new disciples to Baiming Harbor and the start of their Jixia journey. Beneath the bustling surface lies the rich history of the Springbrook Plains. The harmonious blend of old and new draws generation after generation of Society members in their quest for truth.

Dear my new friend, 
Beneath me lies a legion of Mechanoids, 
Warriors ready for battle, the clanging of gold and iron echoes without end. 
In this vast Stone Extraction Hall, only this corner remains secure—a sorrowful sight. 
I have hidden the treasures my senior and I cherish within the tower's peak. May they serve you well. 
May your world be blessed with peace. 
Then, and only then, will we find solace.

I never expected that one adventure would leave my mentor so badly wounded. I tried more than once to press for details, but she gave me no answer. All I know is that she left Aerdeep Camp. What kind of misfortune could have struck her on that road...? 
 
 
 
Perhaps if I had insisted on going with her, things would not have turned out like this. There are still too many secrets hidden in the East Aerfall Highlands. Without Malva, what future can the Sentinel Expedition Team have? 
 
 
 
Yet, as <69D0FF>Master Malva's</> chosen assistant, her student, the one she entrusted with her teaching. It's only natural for me to carry on the work she left unfinished. 
 
 
 
It falls to me now to keep the Sentinel Expedition Team going. I may not have understood why I wanted so badly to follow in her footsteps, but now I have come to understand the true purpose of a Seeker. 
 
The road ahead will be filled with challenges, but the quest for the <69D0FF>secrets of the Sentinels</> must go on, for truth, and for the mysteries still buried beneath this land.
Here, the Volcanic Stones conceal the source that drives everything.\nIt is essential for future generations to safeguard it to ensure everlasting peace.
I hope my friend, wherever you are, whether in the past or future, you are safe and sound.

Congratulations on your success. 
It's been a long time since we last sparred. I still remember that thrilling match. Your attacks were like a raging dragon, each strike leaving behind a wave of heat. I had to transform and dodge repeatedly, striking back whenever possible. 
We were evenly matched, and at times our blows almost got out of control, nearly overturning Darkpool Camp. 
 
I hope we can find an open place soon where we can fight without restraint. 
 
For now, don't waste any more time. Go explore the <69D0FF>northern Aero Plateau</>!
A dismantling Mechcraft tool, misused to the point of disposal, has been warped and deformed by the recoil it endured, now a mere heap of scrap metal.

October 8th, Minor Cold: 
Since Frost's Descent, I've begun treating my first patient and have had several successful cases. 
Master Tong Bo praised me as a genius for quickly learning to differentiate between various medicines, take pulses, and write prescriptions. 
However, I don't think it's about being a genius - I've just been studying tirelessly, reading those pages over and over. 
Master Tong Bo even expressed hope that I would help spread the Herb Society's reputation far and wide, but I'm not interested in that. 
Still, I felt a sense of happiness when those patients thanked me. 
I can finally start saving people, Mother. If only I had been able to do this back then, I wouldn't have to live with this regret... 
I promise not to let anyone else suffer like we did.

Qing Niang apologize for not keeping my promise to meet you at the pier. However, with the war intensifying, my husband and I decided to fight until the end.

It is difficult for Qing Niang, especially with Zhi being so young, but we believe it is for the greater good...

I wish you and Zhi a safe journey, and may you continue the legacy of Mechcraft for the benefit of our people.

Please don't worry about us.

The black thorns spread, the lake dried up, and the forest caught fire. The Dreamweavers lamented in the fire. 
 
 
 
The black thorns entwined, the mountains crumbled, and the tall towers snapped. The Dreamers trembled and wept in the ruins. 
 
 
 
The black thorns decayed, leaving only dark emptiness in the world. A butterfly fluttered its wings alone, finally coming to rest on the tip of a thorn.

The Mechanoids there must be protecting something valuable. \n \nI will wait here until the Seekers dig something out, and then lure the Mechanoids into attacking them. When the chaos settles, I will have all the treasure. A perfect plan, isn't it?

Red maples drift down into the Forbidden Woods, nourishing its quiet depths.

lighting up the whole forest, and kindling my heart as well.

To spare patients from the torment of pain—that was my purpose when I first took up medicine. I've seen the wounded returning from the battlefield; their suffering is not only of the flesh, but of the fear that lingers even after their bodies are healed. Physical recovery alone cannot reach the root. Only by cutting away the memories of pain itself can one truly save them—so they no longer cling to despair or seek death as release. 
 
(Note added in a different hand) 
Having endured the agony of my own flesh rotting away, I speak from bitter experience. Even when the body mends, the memory of pain clings like maggots to bone... Lately, the old illness has begun to return. And I cannot—I will not—go through that torment again. If only I hadn't been found that day...

Dear Master Shi Yu, 
 
I'm sorry for making you worry. I've been busy working on a Mechcraft to replace my legs, which is why I haven't been around... but today, it's finally finished. 
 
 
 
At first, I fell many times trying to walk, but now I've got the hang of it. Life should return to normal soon. If Tian Ji were here, maybe he'd be cheering me on... 
 
 
 
I still remember when Tian Ji introduced us. It feels like it was just yesterday. As for his disappearance... you still haven't accepted it, have you? I heard you haven't been seen at Yong Sheng lately, and I'm starting to worry. If you see this, please write back soon, okay?

Sorcery is the art of mystery. 
 
 
 
All Sorcery, whether grand or bizarre, hinges on a single word: order. 
 
 
 
To observe the orders of all things, to seek the orders that govern all matters—this is the essence of Sorcery. Yet should you delve into the occult and the obscure, one misstep could plunge you into an abyss from which there is no escape. 
 
 
 
That you should read these words means you are fated to do so. I shall impart this sorcery technique to you, one that will keep your mind clear and evil at bay.

Sima Yi, go home. I've flipped through all the books here. None of them contain what you're seeking.

Firestorms raged, and the fierce battle continued without end. 
Armored troops poured in, and the cold moon shone down on piles of white bones. 
The enemy came in waves, their numbers endless. 
In that moment, the Overlord was ambushed while leading a campaign, his life hanging by a thread as he struggled to escape.

Day and night, loud cries and shifting shadows keep me awake. 
 
Stuck in this cursed place, the never-ending darkness is unbearable. 
 
Even if I reject everything, it doesn't change a thing. 
 
Those people are just clueless pawns... 
 
A single lie can easily change someone's life. 
 
I miss my mother so much, her warm smile and loving eyes—she was the only one who loved me no matter what. 
 
The last page says: 
 
"I hid a treasure in the village... it's my only hope. 
 
The treasure must be returned to its rightful place to end the curse. 
 
Break it, reshape it, and pray... save the souls from the endless darkness."

The Finedream Weaver has not appeared for a long time, and my nightmares grow worse by the day. I fear I can no longer replenish the dream energy consumed by my sorcery on my own. 
 
 
 
I even saw the objects in the camp twist into monsters and lunge at me. Only by spending the last of my fine dream energy did I manage to quell the disturbance. 
 
 
 
Why must nightmares still plague this world? If the Finedream Weaver truly manifested, then they should never have allowed nightmares to torment humankind... 
 
 
 
Once I break through this bottleneck, I will prove just how absurd this so-called balance of dream energy truly is!

Crafted with dragon bone decorations by bellmakers, these chimes were believed to carry prayers. Perhaps the giant dragon bone with those enigmatic textures served a similar purpose...

Phantom Rabbits also keep their distance from the shedding Nightmare Peafowl, and they are the first to flee whenever a fight with the birds breaks out. 
 
 
 
It's said that staring at the face of a Phantom Rabbit for too long can cause hallucinations, and some claim that different Sorcerers perceive these patterns differently based on their power. In some places, Sorcerers use this phenomenon to test students' abilities.

text:
Poria Leaf Cake 
Take three taels of Poria cocos leaves, remove the roots and hearts, and crush them into a paste with honey. Mix with one tael of fine butter and cook in silver utensils until syrupy. Wrap the mixture with fresh perilla leaves, and steam in molds for ninety minutes until cooked. 
 
Note: Linye loves honey and butter. The fresh perilla leaves will enhance the fragrance and cut the richness. This Poria Leaf Cake should delight her. 
 
Note: It turns out she didn't like perilla leaves, so I've replaced them with wormwood. It's a bit sweeter, but it matches my feelings for her perfectly. Just like Linye to know.

August 5th, Sunny 
 
When I was young, people often praised my stamina. Inspired by this, I would try to outpace my classmates on mountain climbs, charging ahead as soon as we started, leaving everyone behind. 
 
 
 
But soon enough, I'd be exhausted, my initial impatience throwing off my breathing. By the time I rested on a rock, several classmates had already passed me. 
 
 
 
After a few experiences like this, I began to instinctively avoid training, and my technique turned into a mental hurdle. 
 
 
 
But thanks to a tip from Senior Zhang, I realized I should study the experiences of those who came before me. Trying to reinvent the wheel only leads to more obstacles. 
 
 
 
I calmed down and began to study the techniques and training guides left by predecessors. 
 
 
 
I started walking on mountain paths, paying attention to how "Qi" affects my movements. 
 
 
 
I practiced steady breathing and observed the mountain terrain. 
 
 
 
When I tried climbing again, I felt that my energy was no longer being wasted but was harmonizing with my body movements. Despite moving faster, my breathing remained steady. 
 
 
 
The fatigue from using brute force gradually disappeared, and my speed increased several times! 
 
 
 
I now have my own understanding of using "Qi," and I believe this is why our teacher takes us climbing to practice martial techniques. 
 
 
 
By reading and then applying the knowledge to practice, I'm starting to grasp the true essence of Martial Arts techniques.
